title: Structs and value semantics
summary: Copies, pointers into slices, maps of structs, and embedding (which is not inheritance).
hints: `Translate`: `for _, p := range pts { p.X += dx }` changes a *copy* and does nothing. Loop with the index and write `pts[i].X += dx`. `Biggest` has the same trap: return `&rects[i]`, never `&r` from a `for _, r := range` loop (that is the address of the loop's copy).

`Restock`: `inv[name].Qty += n` does not compile, because a map element is not addressable (the map may move its entries around). Read the whole struct out, change the copy, write it back: `it := inv[name]; it.Name = name; it.Qty += n; inv[name] = it`. A missing key reads as the zero `Item`, which is exactly the starting point you want.

With embedding, `Dog` gets `Animal`'s fields and methods promoted: `d.Name` and `d.Introduce()` just work. But `Animal.Introduce` calls `Animal.Speak`, always: Go has no virtual dispatch through embedding. To make `d.Introduce()` say `"Rex says Woof"` you must define `Introduce` on `Dog` as well, calling `d.Speak()`. `NewDog` builds `Dog{Animal: Animal{Name: name}, Breed: breed}`.
